scope: On-demand English Physics editions from sixteen arXiv subjects and licensed articles in Physical Review A and B. The public Physics edition covers four arXiv subjects.
design: Use October 7 and 21 to check earlier correct and mistaken selections. Reserve September 9 and 23 before inspecting the new editions. Grade the five highest distinct topics, up to five other topics from the bottom of each ranking, and five source-stratified excluded groups per date. A ranked topic passes when the papers share a physical question and its headline, short summary and full synthesis accurately describe their results. A set needs nine passes out of ten for release. Reader corrections follow grading.
query_recovery: The original weekly arXiv queries exhausted their retries on both dates. Their journal-only editions and replays are retained as failed source observations. The recovery checks every UTC day independently. The reported-results reviewer ran on fresh snapshots. We then ran the original review code against those same items and embeddings. The cases, dates and thresholds were fixed before either complete September edition was examined.

previously_read_cases.original_finding: All five prove convergence bounds for dissipative quantum Gibbs sampling. The brief assigns the mixing, gap and entropy results to their systems and states the temperature and truncation assumptions.

The three architectures target fusion success probability, the resources and fidelity for remote graph states, and repeater entanglement distribution rates. The abstracts do not give the same protocol benchmark across the three. The repaired brief separately attributes the predicted fusion probability, remote-state resource count and simulated repeater rate and fidelity. It identifies the gains as model results.

Each treats the accuracy of dispersive effective interactions against an underlying system. The brief attributes the measured Stark shift to the journal paper, the gate fidelity to a simulation, and the dispersive Rabi benchmarks to the general framework.
All three quantify molecular deuterium fractionation in protostars. The summary distinguishes the species, cloud, and first detection, and reports the LTE and chemical-model qualifications.

The first study controls the spread in stored energy over charging trials. The other two calculate work extractable through collective operations or a boundary. The short summary presents the first study as a result on usable work.

The modular and yoked memory studies report qubit overhead or density. The periodic-geometry result increases distance at fixed qubit count and encoding rate. The headline combines these with a qubit reduction and conflates larger-code projections with simulations.

All three identify or calculate a hybrid-mode splitting. The brief separates the predicted graphene/hBN splitting from the local-field and emission experiments and gives the emitter-specific energies.

All three bound communication costs for a quantum advantage. The costs and comparison protocols are separately attributed. A lower bound against randomized two-way communication also applies to a one-way classical protocol.

The tau-pair study estimates errors on entanglement and Bell-sensitive observables. The rare baryon study projects constraints on weak couplings from decay angles, and the top-quark study uses spin correlations to constrain a different interaction. The common spin-correlation headline overstates what all three evaluate.

The targets are a neutron-star equation of state, stellar atmosphere labels, and oscillation frequencies. The methods all compare estimators with references, but the physical outcomes differ. The text identifies the three benchmarks, respective samples and limitations accurately.

One paper detects an ionized phosphorus species in remnants, one gives a tentative FeS detection in Orion and one infers ionization rates and electron fractions in massive cores. No three share the same species abundance or measured ionization rate.

The common mechanism is deconfinement in compact stars. The actual results concern the accessibility of twin-star branches, shifts of radial oscillation frequencies, and an axion-dependent phase boundary and core size. There is no common three-paper measurement of one of these effects.

At least three papers provide stellar effective temperatures and surface gravities: the PLATO benchmark catalogue and the DESI and Gaia-ESO spectroscopic catalogues. Their methods and calibration roles differ, but the published quantities overlap. The separate isochrone study targets mass, radius and age.

new_partitions.question: Spectroscopic survey pipelines that derive stellar parameters and elemental abundances from survey spectra, validated against external catalogues (DESI with a neural network, Gaia-ESO with The Cannon)
Stellar masses, radii and ages inferred from isochrone grids with model-averaging, validated on asteroseismic stars
A compiled benchmark catalogue of well-characterised stars for PLATO

previously_read_cases.original_finding: A Josephson diode measures rectification, the amplifier optimization studies a pumped gain and reflection landscape, and the junction-chain study predicts linewidths and mode populations. The common circuit technology does not supply a shared outcome.

The studies concern a globular-cluster orbit, early-universe gravitational waves, energetic particles from the young Sun and compact remnants inside neutron stars. The physical systems and testable signals differ.

All four quantify the fidelity of engineered quantum gates under control errors or noise. The brief assigns the measured transmon tolerances to the experiment and the reductions in infidelity and other gate results to calculations.

The proposals concern gas-to-star scaling relations, young massive cluster feedback, chemical inventories and gas flows across scales. The brief correctly labels them as forecasts, but extends the specific multi-line, cloud-scale survey requirement to all four.

The common input is interlayer geometry. The outcomes are electronic topology and spin texture, layer polarization and second-harmonic susceptibility. In particular the MoTe2 paper studies an electric-field response in a given twisted bilayer. The short text attributes a study of variation in stacking or twist to all three.

Each study constructs or characterizes a supercritical crossover in AdS black-hole thermodynamics. The text correctly distinguishes the models, the Lee-Yang and spinodal definitions and the supercritical scaling analysis.

One study calculates a gravitational instability for cold axion matter, one predicts a dark-sector coupling, and another finds fixed points for accelerated expansion. They use axions but supply different outputs. The summary separately attributes the model predictions and identifies their theoretical status.

The photonic experiment produces a vortex chirality selected by the valley. The other studies calculate transverse momentum and spin or localized Floquet states and currents. The headline treats orbital angular momentum as setting a common response sign, including where it is the measured output or no sign rule is reported.

All three calculate when suppressing the slowest mode speeds relaxation. The holographic study also checks overtaking from higher excess free energy. The summary preserves the model dependence and distinguishes linear, nonlinear and detector results.

All three calculate the thermal pressure of a non-Abelian gauge plasma. The repaired brief distinguishes the two gluon-plasma calculations and their lattice comparisons from the supersymmetric model and its mass-prescription dependence.

Each benchmarks approximate ground-state energies against a reference. The summary assigns the H2 error to the molecular calculation and the large-system deviations to the transferred Gross–Neveu circuits and preserves the limit on fixed-accuracy scaling.

The time-delay experiment compares two readouts of the same entangled state. It does not compare classical and entangled probe preparations. The other studies compare probes or sources. The brief extends probe-state advantage to the readout comparison even though the detailed paragraph identifies the two detector schemes.

Two abstracts address polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon emission. The companion fine-structure paper fits gas ionization, density and metallicity from different lines. The three do not report the same PAH response.

All three report stellar rotation periods in populations of cluster members. The large catalog includes other periodic phenomena too, but contains measured stellar rotations. The Lagoon Nebula and Hyades/Praesepe provide age- and population-specific comparisons. Splitting all three removes a valid observational question.

new_partitions.question: Do slowly rotating low-mass stars in older (~Gyr-age) open clusters point to earlier or stronger magnetic braking?
What does a large ground-based catalog of cluster rotation periods offer for future tests of magnetic braking?
What do rotation periods of very young (1-2 Myr) stars in the Lagoon Nebula look like with respect to mass and disks?

previously_read_cases.original_finding: The XY study tests a thermal sampling algorithm against Monte Carlo thermodynamic observables. The quantum Hall and neural-wavefunction work concern variational many-body states. A shared neural approach does not give three comparable thermal or ground-state outcomes.

The studies estimate pulsed heat confinement, the electrostatic near field of an AFM tip, and dipolar extinction peaks. A shared electromagnetic modeling framework does not give three estimates of the same observable.

The papers cover distinct questions including a strange-metal transport regime, pairing and Hall-state competition, optical Hall response, edge gaps and collective modes. No set of three in this batch establishes a shared measured quantity or specific theoretical test.

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: Which mass and mass splitting of inelastic dark matter (endothermic or exothermic) best fit the LZ 248 keV nuclear recoil event, and what do the low- and high-energy sidebands say about it?
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: LZ 248 keV recoil: model fits favor TeV endothermic or tens-GeV exothermic inelastic DM
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Preprints fit LZ's single 248 keV recoil with inelastic DM; results depend on model and halo velocities, and an empty high-energy sideband limits broad spectra.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: All eight preprints reinterpret one LZ-reported nuclear recoil (248±23±23 keV, 2.84 ton-yr xenon exposure) as inelastic DM scattering. Their fits are model-dependent fits to a single event, not detections. Endothermic fits favor TeV masses with splittings of a few hundred keV. 2609.04175 finds δ~370–490 keV for a thermal 1.1 TeV higgsino, depending on the velocity distribution. 2609.06571 reports a profile best fit in the inert doublet model at m_H=1080 GeV and m_A−m_H=369 keV. 2609.09015 finds TeV-scale pseudo-Dirac DM with a GeV dark photon. 2609.09107 allows 1–50 TeV and δ~100–500 keV for magnetic dark baryons. 2609.04181 places δ near the escape-speed limit and predicts annual modulation above 50%. Exothermic fits favor lighter DM: ~30–200 GeV with δ~0.5–1 MeV in 2609.05204, and ~55 GeV in 2609.06640. On sidebands, 2609.04175 reports possible tension for a thermal higgsino with LZ's empty high-energy bin, whose acceptance is not public. 2609.04673 finds that this bin disfavors broadly peaked exothermic spectra. 2609.04673 also notes that the lower-energy null result is consistent with an exothermic peak.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: All eight papers estimate which inelastic particle masses or splittings can produce the same LZ recoil. The text attributes the sideband limits and exothermic mass ranges to their respective models and identifies the observation as a single candidate.

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: Can specific inelastic dark matter models explain the LZ 248 keV high-energy nuclear recoil event while satisfying relic-abundance and direct-detection constraints?
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Inelastic dark matter models claim fits to LZ's single 248 keV nuclear recoil
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Theory preprints report that specific inelastic DM models can produce LZ's single 248 keV recoil (2.6σ) while meeting relic and elastic limits within each model.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: The preprints address one question: can inelastic DM–nucleus scattering account for the single LZ nuclear-recoil event? 2609.07800 quotes it at 248±23stat±23sys keV in 2.84 tonne-year, and 2609.10827 gives a 2.6σ background-only significance. All results are model-dependent theoretical consistency claims, not new measurements. 2609.04144 finds that HC-MDM fits the event while satisfying thermal-relic, elastic and solar-capture limits. In certain limits, the model's splitting and inelastic coupling are representation-independent. It reports that generic Higgsino models fail. 2609.07451 finds that much of the singlet-doublet scalar parameter space fits. Its pure-doublet limit is disfavored by IceCube solar-capture searches. 2609.07800 proposes singlet-doublet pseudo-Dirac fermions with tree-level Z-mediated elastic scattering forbidden and a triplet-generated splitting; the abstract states no explicit fit outcome. 2609.10491 argues that exothermic two-component iDM avoids reliance on the velocity tail and relaxes IceCube bounds. 2609.10827 builds endothermic Z′-mediated scalar iDM in chiral U(1)B−L and notes Z′ collider prospects.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: The five studies test explanations of one LZ recoil. The short summary assigns simultaneous relic-density and elastic-scattering checks to every model. The exothermic study examines the relative occupation and longevity of its two states and the IceCube limit without determining their total thermal relic density.

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: Do current CMB, DESI BAO and supernova data show a nonzero coupling between dark matter and dark energy, in which direction does energy flow, and is the interacting model preferred over ΛCDM?
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Dark-sector coupling fits to DESI DR2: model-dependent shifts, no preference over ΛCDM
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Emergent-DE fits shift coupling >95% CL (DE→DM) with CMB+DESI DR2+SNe, yet Bayesian evidence keeps ΛCDM; a GRB+SN study finds γ consistent with 0.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: Four preprints ask whether DESI DR2 BAO, combined with other probes, requires energy exchange between dark matter and dark energy. The answers depend on the assumed coupling model. In two emergent-DE scenarios, arXiv:2609.04990 finds the interaction posterior shifted from zero at >95% CL whenever Planck 2018 CMB is combined with DESI DR2 or with PantheonPlus, DES-Dovekie or Union3 supernovae. The preferred direction is energy transfer from DE to DM, correlated with lower S8. For Q=Γρ_x, arXiv:2609.05660 reports support for interaction when w_x=−1 or w_x<−1 and all three datasets are combined. In both papers, Δχ²_min and Bayesian evidence still favor ΛCDM (and w0waCDM in 2609.04990). arXiv:2609.04746 fits Fermi GRBs, PantheonPlus, DESI DR2 and cosmic chronometers. It finds γ=1.453^{+1.297}_{−1.597} with PantheonPlus-SH0ES calibration and γ=−0.634^{+1.668}_{−2.486} with PantheonPlus-only (GOLD sample). Both are consistent with zero at 68%, and the result is unchanged with the FULL sample. arXiv:2609.07343 sets up an MCMC test of a conformally coupled scalar-field model, C(φ)∝(1+φ)^m, against the same CMB, DESI DR2 and supernova data; the listed abstract does not report its constraints.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: All four papers fit a dark-sector coupling with DESI and other probes. The headline gives a common model-selection verdict. The conformally coupled paper reports a better chi-squared fit than LCDM and AIC support for many data combinations. Its stored abstract ends before those results.

previous_exact_rank.headline: Model-dependent DM–DE coupling hints in DESI DR2 fits; Bayesian evidence favors ΛCDM

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: Which endothermic (inelastic) dark matter models, with parameters fitted to the LZ 248 keV recoil candidate, can explain it and survive other constraints?
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Model-dependent endothermic dark matter fits to LZ 248 keV recoil face solar and collider tests
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Preprints fit endothermic DM models to LZ's 248 keV candidate. Solar capture excludes thermal Higgsino; other fits face collider and gamma-ray tests.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis:
All four preprints take the single 248 keV nuclear-recoil candidate, LZ230616, as input and fit endothermic dark matter with few-hundred-keV splittings. The candidate was reported by LZ in its extended-energy search.

2609.06760 finds the full-density thermal Higgsino excluded. Its LZ-preferred δ≈0.38 MeV falls below the δ≳0.51–0.56 MeV needed to satisfy IceCube solar-annihilation limits. The pseudo-Dirac and neutron-philic O4 benchmarks stay below IceCube under stated conditions: a bb̄ proxy spectrum, and for O4 an equilibrium assumption.

2609.07138 places a pseudo-Dirac doublet in a Dark-Dimension setup. Its two-bin Poisson diagnostic gives a shallow minimum near (1.35 TeV, 366 keV), and the paper predicts a tungsten rate in CaWO4.

2609.07225 gauges baryon number. At m=1 TeV and δ=300 keV, it fixes (M_ZB, g_B)≈(1.44 TeV, 0.233), a point allowed by current searches. The authors propose a Run-3 dijet reanalysis as decisive.

In 2609.10453, the transition magnetic-dipole fits that impose thermal abundance exceed the H.E.S.S. Einasto line bound by factors of about 11 and 5.5.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: Each study tests an endothermic fit to the same recoil with independent constraints or a target prediction. The synthesis assigns the IceCube exclusion to the full-density thermal Higgsino, the tungsten prediction to the doublet and the gamma-ray bounds to the magnetic-dipole calculation.

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: Theoretical precision bounds for quantum parameter estimation (QFI, Cramér-Rao and Barankin bounds on estimator variance or error)
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: New theoretical bounds on quantum estimation: no asymptotic gain from indefinite causal order
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Four theory preprints derive QFI, Cramér-Rao and Barankin limits; one finds indefinite causal order matches parallel strategies asymptotically for channel estimation.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: All four preprints are theoretical analyses of precision limits in quantum parameter estimation; none reports experiments. arXiv:2609.05355 considers a single parameter encoded in N uses of a finite-dimensional channel. It finds that general indefinite-causal-order (ICO) process matrices give the same optimal QFI as parallel strategies for unitary channels. For noisy channels, it finds the same leading QFI coefficient in both the SQL and Heisenberg regimes, so ICO gives no asymptotic advantage. arXiv:2609.08745 shows that quantum U-statistics for polynomial state functionals are asymptotically efficient. Their leading 1/n variance matches the multiparameter quantum Cramér-Rao limit, and the paper adds Bernstein-type concentration bounds. arXiv:2609.09583 relates thermal-state QFI metrics to signal-induced work. For purely quadratic generators in continuous-variable systems, it proves that the infinite-temperature QFI is at least twice the zero-temperature SLD QFI. arXiv:2609.10157 defines a right-division quantum Barankin bound with analytic Gaussian-state matrices. This bound captures few-shot threshold effects that the quantum Cramér-Rao bound misses.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: All four derive precision or error bounds for quantum estimation. The short summary assigns the causal-order claim to one study, and the detailed account gives its channel assumptions, the U-statistic variance, the thermal bound and the few-shot Barankin example separately.

previous_exact_rank.question: What are the ultimate achievable precision limits (QFI or Cramér-Rao/Barankin-type variance bounds) for estimating parameters of quantum states or channels, and how do these limits depend on the resource, strategy or estimator class?
previous_exact_rank.headline: Theoretical bounds on quantum estimation precision across strategies and estimators

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: Can a specific dark matter particle model explain the LUX-ZEPLIN 248 keV high-recoil event?
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Can DM models explain LZ's 248 keV recoil? Three model-dependent answers, one halo-sensitive
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Three preprints test model-specific answers to the LZ 248 keV event; one needs a large coupling product and a halo speed cutoff, and significances depend on templates.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: All three preprints ask whether a specific dark matter particle model can account for the LUX-ZEPLIN high-energy nuclear recoil event near 248 keV. 2609.04186 proposes an elastic pseudoscalar-pseudoscalar model with a complex-singlet pseudoscalar mediator and a heavy vector-like quark; it reports a recoil spectrum between LZ's elastic O4^v and contact L4^v templates, suggesting a 2.6-3.2σ local significance. 2609.06909 argues that its previously proposed inelastic scalar model in gauged U(1)B-L accounts for the 2.6σ event, with a predicted cross section of about 1e-45 cm² and a Z' resonance test at colliders. 2609.08893 examines ALP-mediated inelastic Majorana scattering and finds only a narrow viable region, using an approximate single-event likelihood, that needs a large coupling product and is highly sensitive to the Galactic halo speed cutoff. All three are theoretical interpretations, not new measurements.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: All three predict whether a particular model can yield the same recoil. The local significance comes from the elastic template comparison. The large coupling and halo cutoff concern the axionlike mediator. The scalar resonance result is identified separately.

previous_exact_rank.headline: Proposed dark matter models explain LZ's 248 keV event only under model assumptions

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: Whether proposed new-physics scenarios (atmospheric neutrino up-scattering, Higgsino inelastic dark matter, elastic neutrino scattering) can explain the isolated LZ230616 nuclear recoil event
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: LZ230616 recoil: neutrino up-scattering allowed, Higgsino and elastic CEvNS disfavored
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Three preprints test the isolated 248 keV LZ230616 event: up-scattering gives a benchmark fit; Higgsino DM (standard halo) and elastic CEvNS are disfavored.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: All three preprints address the isolated LZ nuclear recoil at 248±23±23 keV, where the Standard Model background is very small. 2609.04185 proposes atmospheric-neutrino up-scattering νN→χN with a momentum-dependent pseudoscalar-mediator operator, and reports a benchmark (m_χ≈1.13 GeV, m_φ≈494 MeV, √(y_χ y_u)≈0.33) that accounts for the event and remains allowed by other constraints; χ is left generic. 2609.07807 uses Super-Kamiokande and IceCube atmospheric-neutrino measurements to constrain solar-captured Higgsino dark matter, excluding mass splittings ≲557 keV and disfavoring Higgsino interpretations for standard halo velocities. 2609.10504 finds that kinematics, the accompanying low-energy recoil spectrum and existing constraints exclude elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering in all scenarios considered. The answers differ: one viable model-dependent explanation, two disfavored.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: Each asks whether its mechanism can explain the same event. The allowed neutrino up-scattering benchmark, the standard-halo Higgsino limit and the tested elastic-neutrino exclusions are individually attributed.

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: Can reduced order modelling emulate FAM-QRPA nuclear linear response calculations accurately at much lower computational cost?
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Emulators reproduce FAM-QRPA strength functions at far lower cost in nuclear DFT
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Three preprints ask whether emulators reproduce FAM-QRPA strengths at lower cost; each reports yes within its model-specific training domain (x20 in one).
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: All three preprints are calculational and ask whether reduced-order emulation can replace repeated finite amplitude method QRPA solves. arXiv:2609.03903 builds a reduced-basis emulator with the complex external-field energy as the parameter. It reproduces giant-resonance, low-energy and imaginary QRPA modes when training covers the relevant energy domain. For the Dy K^π=0^+ mode it matches full FAM precision at more than an order of magnitude lower cost. arXiv:2609.07452 reports a greedy snapshot strategy that gives a speed-up of more than an order of magnitude including construction. It is demonstrated across light and heavy nuclei, chiral EFT, shell-model and several EDF frameworks. arXiv:2609.07453 uses a 2D-greedy interpolation for a x20 speed-up, then applies it to Brussels BSk(G) functionals. It finds that the correlation between nuclear-matter incompressibility and the Pb-208 ISGMR centroid does not persist. The abstracts do not specify the hardware on which timings were measured.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: The three calculations compare emulated FAM-QRPA nuclear strength functions with full response calculations. The text distinguishes each speed comparison and identifies the model family used for the lead incompressibility result.

previous_exact_rank.question: How accurately and with what computational speed-up can reduced-order/reduced-basis emulators reproduce FAM-QRPA nuclear linear-response strength functions (and QRPA modes) compared with full FAM calculations?
previous_exact_rank.headline: Reduced-basis FAM-QRPA emulators reproduce strength functions in trained energy ranges

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: Does solar capture of the dark matter that explains the LZ event produce a neutrino signal that IceCube can test?
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Can IceCube test solar capture of LZ-event dark matter? Answers depend on each model
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Three model studies of the LZ 248 keV event give model-dependent IceCube answers: partial exclusion in an SD model, a nonthermal-ansatz limit, a weak scalar signal.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: All three preprints take the LZ 248 keV nuclear-recoil candidate as motivation and ask whether solar capture of the proposed dark matter yields a neutrino signal testable with IceCube. 2609.08993 (spin-dependent singlet-doublet Majorana model on a Higgs blind spot) reports that current IceCube limits already probe part of the LZ-compatible thermal parameter space, while a viable region remains. 2609.09138 (mixing-suppressed inelastic Majorana model) gives a conservative thermalized-population limit of δ=300-301 keV and a nominal limit of δ=331-341 keV under its nonthermal cooling ansatz with tree-level elastic scattering. 2609.10636 (inelastic scalar with a B-3L_τ current, one benchmark) finds an inferred annihilation rate of 0.0404 of the IceCube proxy. All results are calculations, not measurements.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: All three calculate solar-neutrino constraints on an LZ interpretation. The comparison separates a partial exclusion, limits under different cooling assumptions and a single scalar benchmark measured against an IceCube proxy.

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: Do stable vortex solitons exist in geometrically structured photonic lattices (quasicrystal with disclinations, fractal Sierpiński gasket, disclination-fractal), and how does the lattice structure affect their stability?
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Stable vortex solitons in disclination, fractal lattices: theory in two, experiment in one
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Quasicrystal-disclination and disclination-fractal studies report stable vortex solitons in theory; a Sierpiński waveguide-array paper reports experimental corner vortex solitons.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: All three papers ask whether vortex solitons can be stabilized by lattice geometry. Vortex Solitons in Disclination Quasicrystals (2609.03244) proposes Penrose-derived quasicrystals with disclinations of chosen rotational order. It reports two stable soliton classes, in-phase and out-of-phase spot pairs, with stability intervals that broaden as the symmetry order decreases. Stable Vortex Soliton Arrays in Disclination-Fractal Systems (2609.09825) reports stable arrays along domain walls, supported by linear stability analysis and perturbed-propagation simulations. It finds arrays in conventional disclination configurations completely unstable. Thresholdless Corner Vortex Solitons in Fractal Sierpiński Topological Insulators (2609.08344) is the experimental study: it reports corner vortex solitons in laser-written Sierpiński gasket waveguide arrays, forming without a power threshold. The summaries do not state quasicrystal experiments or experimental tests of the disclination-fractal arrays.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: Each study reports stable vortex solitons in a structured optical lattice. The English edition identifies the experiment in the Sierpiński array and the two studies that establish stability through calculations.

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: How memory and nonlinear processing arise from the reservoir's physical dynamics (relaxation, dissipation, feedback) in simulated quantum reservoirs
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Simulated quantum reservoirs trace memory to Liouvillian modes, dissipation and feedback
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Five theory/simulation preprints ask how relaxation, dissipation and delayed feedback generate memory and nonlinearity in quantum reservoirs; none report experiments.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: All five preprints are theoretical or numerical studies asking which physical dynamics of open quantum reservoirs produce task-relevant memory and nonlinear processing, and they give different answers. In driven-dissipative Kerr reservoirs, arxiv:2609.20345 finds enhanced memory near both first-order and continuous dissipative transitions. Its exact post-training Liouvillian-mode decomposition attributes capacity mainly to finite-rate modes and their cross-terms, with weak contribution from the gap mode. arxiv:2609.23429 proposes a Volterra-weight factorization W^(q)=BH^(q) separating input-history pathways from readout visibility, and argues that weak measurement and delayed feedback can activate otherwise invisible covariance modes. arxiv:2609.27072 proposes coherent waveguide-QED feedback to a Kerr resonator. In NARMA-n tasks, the optimal delay approximately tracks the input-product lag. In neutral-atom simulations, arxiv:2609.28441 finds controlled dissipation necessary for the echo-state property and reports Mackey-Glass solutions with N=5 atoms. arxiv:2609.22791 models a Gaussian cavity-magnomechanical reservoir with strong memory, limited nonlinearity, and a measurement-budget-dependent optimal encoding.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: All five studies ask how quantum reservoirs retain and process input history. The synthesis assigns covariance-mode activation to weak measurement and delayed feedback together. The cited response study attributes activation to weak measurement, and gives delayed feedback the distinct role of returning earlier inputs.

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: Can inelastic (endothermic or exothermic) or composite dark matter models explain the LZ 248 keV nuclear-recoil event?
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Inelastic and composite dark matter models proposed for LZ 248 keV recoil candidate
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: LZ's 248 keV nuclear-recoil-like candidate prompts preprints explaining it via endothermic, exothermic or form-factor DM scattering in specific models.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: Four theory preprints ask whether a single LUX-ZEPLIN nuclear-recoil-like candidate, quoted in 2609.25723 at 248±23(stat)±23(sys) keV, can come from dark matter scattering on xenon. They give different model-dependent answers. None reports new data. 2609.23477 attributes it to endothermic hyperfine excitation, pseudoscalar to vector, of a composite dark hadron in PQ-augmented dark QCD. It finds that sub-TeV dark matter with a splitting of a few hundred keV gives an order-one rate in the LZ high-recoil window. 2609.25723 instead uses elastic scattering through a screened charge form factor of a neutral composite baryon. It finds that two Gaussian terms cannot produce a hard spectrum, three yield too few events, and four suffice, realized in SU(4)_D×U(1)_D. For a 200 GeV benchmark normalized to one accepted event, it predicts about 1.5 true recoils beyond the current region of interest. It also predicts diffraction nodes whose recoil energies scale as 1/m_A. 2609.26570 and 2609.28415 propose exothermic downscattering. The first uses δ~1000 keV pseudo-Dirac dark matter of 20–100 GeV, also tied to the Galactic Center excess. The second uses a loop-induced dark-photon portal that it says relaxes IceCube constraints.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: Four models predict a recoil spectrum or rate for the same xenon event. The text distinguishes the screened elastic form factor from endothermic excitation and exothermic downscattering. Its extra recoil prediction is identified as a benchmark normalized to the one event.

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: Molecular gas and metallicity scaling relations of low-metallicity star-forming galaxies at cosmic noon from the ALMA ACE CO(3-2) survey: how do molecular gas content, star formation and metallicity relate in these galaxies?
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: ALMA ACE CO(3-2) tests gas–metallicity scaling in low-mass, sub-solar galaxies at z~2
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: ACE detects CO(3-2) in 17 of 26 z~2–2.5 sub-solar main-sequence galaxies; stellar mass sets O/H scatter; gas masses assume a metallicity-dependent αCO.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: Three preprints from the same ALMA Cycle 11 Large Program (ACE) use Band 3 CO(3-2) observations of main-sequence galaxies at z~2–2.5 with 12+log(O/H)≈8.2–8.6 and 10^9<M*<10^10.5 Msun. The overview (2609.21604) reports 25 galaxies, 17 CO and 17 Band 7 continuum detections. It finds that CO detectability tracks metallicity and stellar mass and that dust detectability tracks SFR and L_IR. It also derives an empirical L'CO(3-2)(M*, SFR, Z) relation. The GFMR paper (2609.20921; 26 galaxies, 17/26 CO detections) finds the smallest scatter in the mass–metallicity relation (σ~0.10), compared with the GFMR (σ~0.11) and FMR (σ~0.13). It attributes this possibly to sensitivity only to CO-bright gas. Within a gas-regulator interpretation, it infers outflow loading η~4. The scaling-relation paper (2609.21072) adopts a metallicity-dependent CO-to-H2 factor. It extends M_mol–SFR and f_gas–sSFR relations about an order of magnitude lower in M* at cosmic noon, finds depletion times of ~1 Gyr and proposes an M_mol(SFR, sSFR) prescription.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: The ACE papers share a survey and the question of how molecular gas, gas metallicity, stellar mass and star formation relate. The account gives the separate 25- and 26-galaxy samples and states the CO conversion assumption and the dependence on CO-bright gas.

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: Lensing deflection angles, strong-lensing observables and EHT shadow-based parameter bounds for black holes in modified gravity or with a hair or dark matter parameter, where Sgr A* shadow constraints are common to all three
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Model-conditional EHT Sgr A* shadow bounds on black hole hair, charge and dark matter
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Three theory preprints model lensing and shadows of dyonic, primary-hair and STVG–PFDM black holes; Sgr A* shadow bounds hold only within each assumed metric.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: All three preprints are theoretical calculations that take published EHT shadow sizes as external inputs. None reports new observations. Each paper's parameter bound is conditional on its assumed metric. For a dyonic black hole in Kalb-Ramond gravity, arXiv:2609.21990 obtains matching weak-deflection angles from the Gauss-Bonnet, orbit-equation and Fermat-principle methods. It also gives strong-deflection coefficients via Tsukamoto's method. From Sgr A* and M87* shadows it derives conditional charge bounds, supplemented by an S2-precession estimate. Within that model, it constructs strong-lensing observable combinations that separate the effective charge from the conical parameter. arXiv:2609.25667 studies a gravitational-decoupling primary-hair Schwarzschild deformation. It finds that the coupling α dominates the leading-order deflection and that the hair Q acts repulsively. It constrains Q for several α values using the Sgr A* shadow. arXiv:2609.28583 maps EHT-compatible regions in (a, α) for a rotating STVG–PFDM black hole at representative λ values. It finds that PFDM shifts the allowed region and that shadow size is less sensitive to spin than to deformation. It also computes Hawking emission and eikonal quasinormal modes.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: All three calculate a shadow size and compare it with Sgr A* to constrain a model parameter. The scope and any additional M87*, stellar-orbit or quasinormal-mode results are attached to the appropriate metric.

previous_exact_rank.headline: Model-dependent EHT shadow bounds on non-Schwarzschild black hole parameters, from theory-only calculations

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: What is the overall design of the CMS HL-LHC heterogeneous tracking sequence (Patatrack and LST on GPU, mkFit on CPU), and what does it achieve?
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: CMS Phase-2 tracking baseline pairs GPU Patatrack/LST seeding with vectorized CPU mkFit
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Three CMS papers outline the proposed HL-LHC tracking sequence; abstracts claim reduced resource needs and added displaced tracking but quote no figures.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: All three preprints are CMS contributions describing the same proposed Phase-2 baseline track reconstruction for HL-LHC pileup conditions. It combines Patatrack and Line Segment Tracking (LST), designed for parallel or GPU execution, with mkFit, vectorized for CPUs. 2609.20135 and 2609.26383 frame it as the online baseline; 2609.20135 also names the main offline iteration, while 2609.26383 says it could be similarly useful offline. 2609.26376 focuses on the High Level Trigger: mkFit, used in Run 3, performs pattern recognition on Patatrack and LST seeds. It also applies deep neural networks and multi-objective particle swarm optimization to suppress duplicate and fake tracks. 2609.20135 and 2609.26383 state that the sequence reduces resource requirements and adds global displaced tracking. 2609.26383 links this to long-lived-particle sensitivity. The abstracts give no efficiencies, fake rates, timings or hardware models. Their performance claims therefore cannot be tied to specific simulated samples or devices.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: All three describe the same CMS Phase-2 tracking sequence. The account identifies the common online application, the different claims about offline use, GPU-suitable seed finding and vectorized CPU pattern recognition. It explicitly identifies these as contributions from one collaboration.

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: What singularity scaling (Kasner) exponent can be extracted from black hole interior probes such as asymptotic quasinormal modes or holographic correlator singularities?
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Singularity scaling exponents from QNM offsets and bouncing correlator poles in model black holes
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Two QNM papers (2+1D AdS quantum BHs; one assuming Stokes topology) and one holographic study of truncated blackening factors relate probe data to singularity exponents.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: The shared question is which singularity scaling or Kasner exponent can be read from black hole interior probes. arXiv:2609.20788 shows how to extract the singularity's scaling exponent from the large-overtone QNM spectrum of a massless scalar, applied to exact (2+1)-dimensional AdS quantum black holes, and reports a deep-interior transition as quantum effects dominate. arXiv:2609.26724 treats the same class of semi-classical solutions with complex-analytic methods, finds leading frequencies of the form offset plus n times gap, and reconstructs the exponent from the offset under an assumed global Stokes topology. It also uses subleading corrections, links the transition to Kasner eons, and reports a charged-case crossover with oscillations that may signal the inner horizon. arXiv:2609.23776 is a holographic analysis of black branes with truncated blackening factors, relating bouncing-singularity exponents in thermal two-point functions to the time-direction Kasner exponent, with a stated regime of validity.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: The output in each model is information about a black-hole singularity exponent. The two quasinormal-mode studies and the holographic correlator study use different probes. The synthesis distinguishes them and includes the Stokes-topology assumption.

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: How work and ergotropy can be extracted from quantum batteries
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Three theory studies on quantum-battery work extraction: scar steering, pointer feedback, bosonic entanglement
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Three theoretical papers ask how work is extracted from quantum batteries: scar-state steering, pointer feedback, and entanglement-limited bosonic charging.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: The three preprints are theoretical and address work and ergotropy extraction from quantum batteries; none reports an experimental measurement. arXiv:2609.20966 proposes a dissipation-plus-continuous-indirect-measurement protocol that steers a many-body battery into one scar state, from which local unitaries extract work. arXiv:2609.24425 analyzes a two-level battery with a Gaussian pointer and finds that daemonic ergotropy equals standard ergotropy for the pure initial state at all interaction strengths; it describes the scheme as amenable to trapped-ion implementation. arXiv:2609.26573 gives exact dynamics for a bosonic battery charged by a coherent-state superposition, linking extractable-work loss to charger-battery entanglement. Under single-photon loss, the analytical structure survives, but charger disentanglement and maximal work extraction separate.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: The three analyses estimate extractable work from a quantum battery. The short and long accounts attribute scar-state steering, a conditional pointer and entanglement-dependent losses to their respective models.

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: Theoretical quasinormal mode frequencies of modified black hole spacetimes: how do environmental or boundary modifications (near-horizon reflective surface in Schwarzschild-AdS, Kiselev/Rastall matter and charge, galactic halo) change the QNM spectrum compared with the standard black hole?
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Theoretical QNM spectra shift with horizon, matter and halo modifications in model-specific ways
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Three theory papers compute how a near-horizon surface, Kiselev–Rastall matter with charge, or a halo with radial pressure alters black-hole QNMs, each in its own model.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: All three preprints are theoretical and numerical studies of how modifying the standard black-hole setting changes quasinormal frequencies; none reports an observational measurement. arXiv:2609.20382 solves scalar modes of Schwarzschild-AdS with a partially reflective near-horizon surface by Chebyshev collocation, finding cavity-like, roughly equally spaced sequences at large real part, a weakly damped quasibound branch at large AdS radius, and strong sensitivity to the boundary condition. arXiv:2609.25565 treats axial perturbations of charged Kiselev black holes in Rastall gravity, proves axial mode stability under its adopted closure, and gives fundamental frequencies from a Chebyshev pseudospectral calculation over the parameter ranges examined. arXiv:2609.27379 derives, in the eikonal limit, a universal redshift of real and imaginary QNM parts for dilute halos with w≠-1, breaking at w=-1; its scalar-field numerics confirm the analytic results.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: Each paper computes a quasinormal-mode frequency spectrum after changing a black-hole boundary or matter model. The synthesis keeps the three settings distinct and preserves the dilute-halo and equation-of-state restrictions on a common redshift.

previous_exact_rank.question: How do modifications to the black-hole environment or boundary conditions (a near-horizon reflective surface, surrounding Kiselev/Rastall matter, galactic halo matter) shift the quasinormal-mode frequencies and damping rates relative to the vacuum or standard black hole?

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: First-passage and survival statistics of diffusive particles under stochastic resetting: how resetting changes the time for a diffusing particle to be absorbed or to survive, including whether an optimal resetting rate exists
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Theory: resetting shifts first-passage and survival in model diffusers, with optimal rates in two
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Three analytical studies ask how resetting alters absorption or survival; two find optimal or beneficial rate windows, one finds drift-dependent exponential decay.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: The three preprints are theoretical analyses of how stochastic resetting changes absorption or survival of a diffusing particle; none reports an experimental measurement. arXiv:2609.21124 treats a weakly active Ornstein–Uhlenbeck particle on a finite interval by perturbation theory and renewal methods. It finds a finite range of resetting rates that lowers the mean first-passage time, with the transition depending on the velocity resetting protocol. arXiv:2609.22527 derives exact Laplace-space survival results for a delta killing trap. Without resetting, drift leaves nonzero ultimate survival; with r>0 and k>0, survival decays exponentially. arXiv:2609.24427 treats 2D heterogeneous diffusion with D(ρ)=D0/ρ², under Itô, Stratonovich and Hänggi–Klimontovich prescriptions. It reports an optimal resetting rate that minimises the mean first-passage time, and the rate rises as the memory exponent falls in the subordinated model.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: Each analytic model studies absorption or survival under resetting. The text distinguishes the interval in which resetting helps, long-time exponential survival for the killing trap and the calculated optimum in the heterogeneous planar model.

previous_exact_rank.question: How does the stochastic resetting rate control the first-passage or survival time to an absorbing target for a diffusing particle, including whether and where resetting reduces the mean first-passage time?
previous_exact_rank.headline: Resetting rate sets where mean first-passage time falls, depending on the model

unannotated_editorial_cases.question: How much do lensing systematics or degeneracies (subhalo perturbations, mismodelled lens components, shape degeneracies) change predicted or inferred time delays and the quantities derived from them?
unannotated_editorial_cases.headline: Subhalos, mismodelling and shape degeneracies shift lensed time delays by model-dependent amounts
unannotated_editorial_cases.summary: Simulated NFW subhalos give hour-scale GW delay shifts; modified-gravity D is biased by mismodelling; analytic shape degeneracies shift MACS J0416-like delays ~1–10%.
unannotated_editorial_cases.synthesis: The three preprints ask how lensing systematics or degeneracies alter time delays and quantities derived from them, with different answers. 2609.23428 simulates 10^6–10^9 Msun NFW subhalos in fold and cusp galaxy-lens configurations (200 realisations each) and finds hour-scale perturbations to macro-image delays, with no milli-images produced. 2609.24351 uses a simulated BNS sample, NFW cluster halos and an SIS BCG, assuming 5 per cent time-delay-span precision. Within its gravity model, neglected ellipticity, secondary structure, mis-centring and line-of-sight perturbations bias the inferred modified-gravity parameter D, while BCG and redshift uncertainties are subdominant. 2609.27147 is an analytical study proposing shape degeneracies as the likely cause of mass-map differences; for high-image-number clusters such as MACS J0416 it reports delay effects of order 1%, reaching ~10% for some sources, affecting H_0. None is an observational measurement.
unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: All three model lens time delays or the parameter bias inferred from those delays. The synthesis keeps the hour-scale perturbations, the bias in D and the percent-scale shape-degeneracy effect separate and identifies the simulated or analytical setting.

unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: Two studies model the intergalactic medium during reionization. The third estimates the present-day warm-hot baryon fraction and its numerical-resolution dependence. That result does not provide a third estimate of a reionization observable.

The maser and disk studies relate line variability to changing accretion. The brown-dwarf study instead measures a rotational period and the amplitude of atmospheric modulation. A change between observing epochs alone cannot supply a common physical question.

All three evaluate machine-learning recovery of strong lenses on Kilo-Degree Survey imaging. LenNet detects and localizes lenses directly, but it is also tested on real KiDS lenses. A comparison can distinguish its localization task and the different validation samples.

unannotated_editorial_cases.finding: Quantized transverse soliton velocity, separation of cooling times and photon antibunching are different physical outcomes. Lattice dynamics or dissipation appear in the models but do not provide a shared measurement.

The four papers constrain annihilation using 21-cm forecasts, thermal relics using the Lyman-alpha forest, stellar heating in white dwarfs and a reionization optical depth using the CMB. No three report a common physical constraint on the same quantity.

calibration_result: Of ten previously judged coherent ranked groups, six retained exactly the same papers. Two of ten previously judged incoherent ranked groups also retained exactly the same papers. Neither known group of three comparable stellar measurements was recovered. The new output descriptions identify the shared temperatures, surface gravities or rotation periods, but the review still separated papers by survey, age or method.

cost.method: Sum new token-ledger amounts only, subtracting the inherited balance on every replay. A charge for an API or SDK failure without returned usage cannot be measured from the ledger. Costs are retrospective pilot measurements. The total monthly budget still requires live measurement.
cost.billing_limit: A response rejected during SDK parsing can lack a token count. Twenty-four root validation warnings were logged. The provider charge for these responses cannot be distinguished in the recorded usage. Retry responses with returned counts are included.

reading_copy_integrity: Across both corrected English editions the retained raw data matched the graded snapshots byte for byte (1,968 files for September 9 and 2,067 for September 23). The audit only rebuilt the dated English reading copies.
september_9_recheck: Two initial review decisions failed validation and were retried without recollecting papers or changing embeddings. Both reviewers independently retried the one first-stage decision. Both excluded it, so all 41 proposed memberships matched. The revised replay recovered a four-paper topic. All 15 selected September 9 cases retained the same editorial text and supporting papers after recovery. The five sampled lower ranks moved down one place.
publication_decision: Keep expanded Physics on demand. The regular Physics edition still takes four arXiv subjects. Review the missed comparable measurements, mixed outcomes and source omissions before changing the public scope. New public fields also require fourteen actual shared operating dates and a measured total budget.
